text.title: Freelancer Scope-Change Script Library Core Rules
text.summary: Seven rules constraining every script in the library: the impact line must price both money and schedule, the option set must include a swap that keeps the date, work waits on a written change order, mission-creep scripts cite the running total, and emergency scripts declare their own end.

rule.statement: impact_line MUST quantify the money delta and the schedule delta together, each with a unit and a reference point — "+14 h / +EUR 1,400, and it moves launch from 12 to 19 June". An impact line naming only one of the two is rejected.

rationale.source: PMBOK Guide — Perform Integrated Change Control (cost and schedule impact assessed together)

rule.rationale: Stated alone, a price invites "can you just squeeze it in", and a date alone invites "take the extra week, same budget". Only both together present the request as a trade with two axes, which is what stops the client from paying on the axis they consider cheap.

rule.statement: options MUST contain at least two named options, and at least one of them keeps the original deadline and budget by deferring a specific in-scope item that the script names. An option set that only offers "more money" and "more time" fails.

rationale.source: MESO — Multiple Equivalent Simultaneous Offers (negotiation practice)

rule.rationale: A single path is heard as an ultimatum and gets counter-negotiated on price. The swap option makes the fixed capacity visible without the freelancer refusing anything: the client picks which existing item loses, so the trade-off is theirs and the boundary holds without a "no".

rule.statement: For situation_type big-ask and mission-creep, next_step MUST name a written artefact (change-order email to be confirmed by reply, signed CR, amended SOW line) and a decision deadline date. "I'll start and we'll sort the paperwork later" is forbidden in those two types.

rationale.source: Change-order practice in contract administration (AIA / construction and consulting contracts)

rule.rationale: Work done before the change order is unbilled by default, so its invoice arrives as a surprise after the value has already been delivered and the client's leverage is at its highest. The same amount agreed in advance is a routine line item; agreed after, it is a dispute.

rule.statement: For situation_type mission-creep the script MUST state the cumulative figure — how many prior unbilled asks and how many hours across them — not just the current request. The count and hours come from a log the operator keeps, and the script quotes it verbatim.
rule.rationale: Each ask is individually small and individually reasonable, and compliance with the previous ones is exactly what makes the next one easier to make. The client has no view of the aggregate, so declining the current small ask on its own looks disproportionate; the running total is the only evidence that reframes the conversation from this request to the pattern.

rule.statement: For situation_type emergency the script MUST bound the concession in the same message: an end date or hour count, and the named in-scope item that gets dropped or delayed to make room. Open-ended offers of help ("I'll take care of it") are rejected.

rationale.source: Internal — retainer and out-of-hours boundary practice

rule.rationale: Nobody sends a notification when the emergency is over, so an unbounded concession quietly becomes the baseline expectation and the next request arrives against the new normal. Declaring the end while the goodwill is being spent is the only moment where the boundary costs nothing.

rule.statement: empathy_line acknowledges the client's pressure and stops there: it contains no apology ("sorry for the hassle"), and no commitment verb before the option set ("no problem", "happy to fit it in", "of course"). Checkable by scanning for those tokens.

rationale.source: Voss, Never Split the Difference — labelling the counterpart's position without conceding

rule.rationale: An apology accepts fault for a change the client requested, which moves the price argument onto your side of the table. A concession offered before the impact line has priced the change sets that price at zero — the options that follow read as an attempt to walk back an offer already made.

rule.statement: Skip when there is no commercial scope boundary to defend (internal-team work) or when the situation is termination or a payment default rather than a scope change — those route to contract review, not to a script. Emit a structured skip naming which condition held.
rule.rationale: These scripts work by pricing a change against an agreed baseline. Where no baseline exists, or where the dispute is about the contract itself, a well-phrased option set commits the operator to a position before anyone has read the terms.
